src.t.1cttcm9: Breadth-first: everything one link away first, then everything two links away. Like gossip: first the neighbours hear it, then their neighbours.
src.t.4iie8v: An inverted index is the index at the back of a book: for every word, the pages it is on.
src.t.1mc1xj6: PageRank: a page matters if pages that matter link to it. Like a tea house that the best tea houses send people to.
src.t.qmjkr: p95: ninety-five answers in a hundred come faster than this. The slow five are the ones people complain about.
src.t.1t8rfl6: Transcoding re-encodes each upload once for every size on the ladder. The player then picks the rendition the connection can carry.
src.t.6zng33: The origin is the one real copy of every video. Every edge just keeps copies of what is popular nearby.
src.t.1dssk97: A viral hit was watched by everyone, so by raw counts it looks like everything. It would follow every single video.
src.t.14zbu5t: Skip-gram: from one word, guess its neighbours. Words that keep the same company end up with similar vectors.
src.t.1s58yp9: The checkpoint is the trained weights on disk, one row per vocabulary word. Change the vocabulary and the rows no longer line up.
src.t.1imagoe: The embedding table has one row of numbers per token. More tokens, a bigger table, and rare rows that hardly ever get trained.
src.t.cu7yg6: LoRA trains two thin matrices beside the big frozen ones. A small add-on instead of a whole new model.
src.t.ev8uvb: Contrastive training pulls each picture towards its own caption and pushes it away from all the other captions in the batch.
src.t.1sfua04: System 1 is the quick gut feeling, System 2 the slow careful thinking. We train the first to copy the second.
src.t.xux92w: A schema is a lab’s idea of what an answer looks like: where the text goes and what the token counts are called.
src.t.thuo9f: Gravity: every frame Sam falls a little faster, 0.4 pixels per frame more. Fall for a while and he is quick.
src.t.121fley: Terminal speed: 14 pixels a frame. A plank is only 2 pixels thick, so that is a very long step to take in one go.
src.t.18tvulj: A speed limit on one frame’s move, smaller than the thinnest floor. It is safe, but Sam falls like a feather.
src.t.18ekpqo: A swept test: slide Sam down the path pixel by pixel and stop at the first floor. Nothing on the way can be skipped.
src.t.1qt1xuh: A discrete test: look only where Sam ended up, and if that is inside a floor, push him back on top. If he jumped clean over the plank, it sees nothing.
src.t.gtkj0v: landed says whether Sam stands on something this frame. Only then may he jump.
src.t.ide7b: vy is Sam’s vertical speed in pixels per frame. Positive is down.
src.t.1as5c4z: y is the top of Sam’s hitbox, in pixels from the top of the level. Bigger is lower.
src.t.1brl3vd: OAM is the little list the picture chip reads its sprites from: 64 slots of 8-pixel pieces.
src.t.1ncaf30: The chip can draw only 8 sprite pieces on one scanline, one row of the picture. The ninth is skipped, silently.
src.t.4e14ba: Who loses when a line is full? The same sprite every time, so it vanishes, or in turns, so everyone just blinks a bit.
src.t.ocdwk5: oam-order: the list as it was made. rotate: start from a different sprite every frame. hero-rotate: Sam first, everyone else in turns.
src.t.cqsswy: How big a bug is. A 16 by 16 sprite is two pieces wide on every line it covers, an 8 by 8 only one.
src.t.14807mx: Swarm: every bug at once. Waves: a few at a time, so the lines stay emptier.
src.t.1jvs0aj: The fastest any road gets: a highway costs 0.45 of a street per metre. A guess built on it can never be too pessimistic.
src.t.1noniv7: estimate guesses the cost still to go from a straight line at highway speed. It must never claim more than the truth, or the search stops trusting the best road.
src.t.llc51q: The open list: junctions we know how to reach but have not visited yet, with the most promising one on top. What goes in as its priority is the whole algorithm.
src.t.uy8ne2: road.time is what the road costs to drive: its length divided by how fast it goes. A highway is cheap, an alley is dear.
src.t.14l05dt: g is the cost so far to get to each junction by the best way found yet.
src.t.1qliwjy: One physics step is always a sixtieth of a second, whatever the frame time. The same input gives the same result.
src.t.2ww4l2: If a frame took longer than this, pretend it did not. Otherwise catching up takes longer than the frame itself and the game never recovers.
src.t.erim6i: The accumulator: time that has passed but physics has not yet simulated. Each step takes one STEP out of it.
src.t.xpdrai: integrate moves everything on by one slice of time: new position is old position plus speed times time.
src.t.1v37gb5: The city is cut into square chunks of this many metres. Big chunks mean long loads that stall a frame; tiny ones mean lots of bookkeeping.
src.t.jei3x: How many chunks around the van are kept loaded. Too few and buildings pop in; too many and the memory runs out.
src.t.1j1ky9d: How many levels of detail the chunks come in. With more, the rings far from the van are loaded as cheap blobs and use a sixteenth of the memory.
src.t.6t0myr: Also load the chunks where the van will be in two and a half seconds. Fewer pop-ins, a bit more memory.
src.t.133afl4: surrounding finds the two keys either side of this frame. Everything between them is the computer’s job.
src.t.zhui6v: Keys are the poses the animator set by hand: here at frame zero, here at the top of the hop. The computer invents the frames in between.
src.t.kc9c49: u is how far we are between the two keys: nought on the first, one on the second.
src.t.1ylb33j: A cubic Bézier bends a path with two handles. Put the handles flat at the top of a hop and the glass slows down there, like a real thing thrown up.
src.t.v176e7: The handles on each key. How long they are and which way they point decide how the motion eases in and out.
src.t.1iqhjpf: A spline that passes through the keys using the neighbouring keys to guess the direction. Stretch its tangents (the 2.4) and it swings past the key.
src.t.lo21nn: The bones that pull on this vertex. Near the joint it has two: the one below and the one above.
src.t.1s4va5s: How hard this bone pulls on this vertex. Zero means not at all, one means it follows the bone exactly.
src.t.u3ml3z: The weights of one vertex added up. If you paint by hand it drifts away from one, and then the vertex lands in the wrong place.
src.t.1ei0c6i: The bone’s current matrix: where it is and how it is turned in this frame.
src.t.d2z5te: Where the vertex sits when the character stands in his rest pose, before anything moves.
src.t.18zs7n: Only the bone with the highest weight is allowed to move this vertex. Simple, and it makes a hard crease at the joint.
src.t.17orcnd: N dot L: how squarely the light lands. Straight on is one, sideways is nought. Lambert’s law, 1760.
src.t.15puavo: HZ: how many times a second the timer interrupt fires. Each one checks whether a slice is over and costs a bit of time. 100 is lazy, 1000 is alert.
src.t.1vteq1q: How easily the kernel itself can be interrupted: never inside a system call, at marked places, or almost anywhere. Easier means snappier, and a bit slower overall.
src.t.18flpdf: The governor sets the CPU speed. powersave is slow and cool, performance is flat out and hot, schedutil follows the load.
src.t.1h845p1: Money is a plain number, but what it counts matters: whole kuruş, an integer, never lira with decimals.
src.t.6awnh1: Today’s dollar rate. Tourists pay in dollars and we convert, so every dollar order is rounded once, here, on purpose.
src.t.1fwszcv: The fee the bank takes: 2.9 percent plus thirty kuruş. Round it the way the bank does, or the books drift.
src.t.1tvbnug: 0.029 is 2.9 percent as a fraction. Multiply an amount by it and you get the percentage part of the fee.
src.t.zq7rgh: total adds up a list of amounts. With whole kuruş the sum is exact; with decimals every addition can add a tiny error.
src.t.klwv2c: An entry is one line in the ledger: an account and an amount. Plus is a credit, minus a debit.
src.t.1bpg9ga: A debit takes money out of an account, a credit puts it into another. Every payment is both, together, and they sum to zero.
src.t.hbvry: commit writes all the entries in one transaction: all of them happen or none do. No half-written payments.
src.t.dnba77: A balance is a number that just goes up and down. Nothing records where the money came from, so nothing can be checked.
src.t.hy0t7: Three separate writes. If the server dies after the first, the other two never happen and the money has simply gone.
src.t.1g7xus: fee is our cut taken from the merchant’s share. It gets its own account, so we can see how much we have earned.
src.t.1z0eezt: The idempotency key is a ticket number the phone makes up for each purchase and repeats on every retry. Same ticket, same answer.
src.t.ycb5tg: The store is our memory of requests we have already answered. We look there before touching the customer’s money.
src.t.19zcc8h: This is the call that actually takes the money. It must happen once per purchase, however often the phone asks.
src.t.8da7uq: refuse turns the customer away. Used on guesses, it also turns away someone who really wanted a second tea.
src.t.1vocudh: A ChargeRequest is what the phone sends: the card, the amount, and the idempotency key.
src.t.1j8wroh: Backoff is how long to wait before asking again. Waiting longer each time gives a struggling bank room to breathe.
src.t.1pzwyej: Jitter adds a random bit to each wait, so four hundred clients do not all come back in the same second.
src.t.qifh5m: How many times a client asks before giving up. Too few and an outage loses sales; unlimited and a dead bank gets hammered forever.
src.t.50m40o: The fraud score above which a payment is blocked. Lower catches more fraud and blocks more honest customers too.
src.t.1p0ct9b: The 3-D Secure step: in the grey zone the customer gets a code from their bank. Honest people type it; thieves do not have the phone.
src.t.1ddhwyi: A page is one block of the index, as big as a disk read. Each holds a sorted run of keys, and a tree of pages is the whole index.
src.t.12dozaa: A key is what the index is sorted by, here the row’s id. Finding a key is walking down from the root, a few pages deep.
src.t.qiht2c: take copies a slice of the page’s keys, from the first number up to, not including, the second.
src.t.13mf9hk: mid is where the page is cut. Everything before it goes left, everything from it onwards goes right, and no key may be left out.
src.t.pwjjjp: cut is a cut at one fifth of the page. The left page is nearly empty from the day it is born.
src.t.12syn1y: sep is the separator the parent keeps: keys below it are in the left page, keys from it up are in the right one.
src.t.1tr0sr0: The LSN, log sequence number, counts the log’s records. Each change gets the next number, so “which came first” is never in doubt.
src.t.1vinsm: append adds the record to the end of the log. At this point it is only in memory, the operating system’s notebook, not on the disk.
src.t.1ndpdvs: fsync makes the operating system actually write to the disk and wait for it. It costs a couple of milliseconds, and it is the only real promise.
src.t.1j0pkbs: Rewriting the table’s pages directly. If the power dies halfway through a page there is nothing to say what it should have contained.
src.t.b2ftq1: ack tells the client “committed”. After that we owe them: that data must survive anything.
src.t.1331rqm: A Tx is one transaction: a group of changes that must happen together or not at all.
src.t.d0lkqp: The set of transactions whose commit record reached the log. Those are the ones we promised to keep.
src.t.1sctub5: The number of this log record. Compare it with the page’s own number to see whether the page already has this change.
src.t.yxdaar: Each page remembers the number of the last change it holds. That is how recovery knows which records were already applied.
src.t.1nbj0l7: redo applies a logged change to a page again, as it was the first time. Doing it for a change the page already has would apply it twice.
src.t.kxpu0: N dot H: how close the surface is to the exact mirror angle between the light and your eye. Close means a glint.
src.t.1hw2mwk: Fresnel: glass reflects only 4 percent of the light looking straight at it, nearly all of it at a grazing angle. Whatever it reflects, the diffuse part does not get.
src.t.gkjrps: How tight the glint is. A high number is a small sharp spot, a low one a wide soft glow.
src.t.4ti9uv: The surface’s own colour: the share of the light it does not absorb.
src.t.1seh1ss: The halfway vector sits exactly between the light and your eye. When it points along the normal, you see the glint.
src.t.jubwyv: The numbers the light maths is done in. Light adds up properly only in linear numbers, where double the light is double the number.
src.t.1xjfuko: What happens at the very end, when the picture goes to the screen. Screens expect numbers squeezed through a curve; sRGB is that curve.
src.t.13car9o: Light has no ceiling but a screen does. The tone-map decides how a very bright pixel gets squeezed under it.
src.t.1x7juwg: Clip chops everything above white. Reinhard squeezes everything a little. Filmic leaves the middle alone and rolls the top off gently, like film.
src.t.1nz5i2u: A rough sRGB: raise to the power one over 2.2. Close, but not the real curve.
src.t.1hjsqjd: Machines rendering at the same time. You pay for each one for as long as the farm runs, busy or idle.
src.t.1nq4i: How frames are handed out. Fixed blocks give each node its stretch up front; a shared queue gives the next frame to whoever is free.
src.t.10w032f: With a queue nobody sits idle while another node chews the expensive splash scene. With fixed blocks, whoever draws the splash is late.
src.t.uce9u7: On-demand machines never go away; spot ones are about a third of the price, but may be taken back, and the frame they were on is rendered again.
src.t.17a333i: With the cache on, a node keeps the scene in memory. Off, it loads textures and geometry again for every single frame, thirty-odd seconds each.
src.t.19g9f95: The model matrix puts one object into the world: where it stands, how it is turned, how big it is.
src.t.1hcj929: The view matrix moves the whole world so that the camera sits at the origin looking down the minus z axis. Moving the camera is moving everything else the other way.
src.t.pik0wr: The projection matrix squeezes the camera’s view into a box and stores the distance in w, so that the divide later can make far things small.
src.t.l4c91n: The nearest and the farthest distance the camera can see. Anything outside is cut off. Too wide a range and the depth numbers run out of precision.
src.t.pglen4: Matrix multiplication. It is not commutative: A times B is not B times A. The one nearest the vertex is applied first.
src.t.1q6xipy: Model, view and projection multiplied into one matrix, so each vertex needs only one multiplication instead of three.
src.t.y2pptl: Clip space: the numbers straight out of the projection matrix, before the divide. Inside the view if x, y and z are between minus w and w.
src.t.2tntgl: toScreen turns clip-space numbers into pixel positions: first the perspective divide, then stretch minus-one-to-one onto the screen size.
src.t.13gxfsb: Normalised device coordinates: x, y and z all between minus one and one, whatever the screen size. A box every camera view is squeezed into.
src.t.5d1hac: w is the distance from the camera, kept by the projection matrix for exactly this moment. z is not the distance: z is already a squeezed depth.
src.t.g6ge8r: Barycentric coordinates: how much of each corner a point is made of. All three positive means the point is inside the triangle.
src.t.1gn6j6v: How far this triangle is from the camera at this pixel, blended from its three corners.
src.t.mhncmj: Colours one pixel on the screen. Everything before it was deciding whether we should.
src.t.1ghc275: One physics step: one sixtieth of a second, always. The same step on every machine means the same game on every machine.
src.t.cfoe49: The accumulator: the real time that has passed but has not been simulated yet. We spend it in whole steps and keep the leftover.
src.t.1wvvf7t: update moves the game forward by some seconds: physics, AI, the lot.
src.t.bftvqc: dt is the real time the last frame took. It jumps around: 7 milliseconds on a fast machine, 33 on a slow one, 400 when the laptop remembers it has updates.
src.t.1bg8z7j: The leftover, as a fraction of a step, goes to the renderer so it can draw things between two physics states, smoothly.
src.t.paw92d: Back-face culling: a triangle seen from behind is the inside of something solid, so you skip it. Which side is the front is decided by the winding: counter-clockwise by convention.
src.t.9vydc6: Counter-clockwise or clockwise: the order of the three corners on screen. Most engines call counter-clockwise the front.
src.t.14uqkbp: The frustum is the pyramid-shaped box the camera sees. Objects wholly outside it are never sent to the GPU.
src.t.1k7c51p: How to test an object against the frustum. A bounding sphere or box is safe. Testing only the centre makes objects vanish while half of them are still on screen.
src.t.cipwfj: The share of the screen’s pixels we render. A sixth fewer pixels is a sixth less pixel work, and a softer picture.
src.t.glejmg: Level of detail: far away objects use a simpler model, because you cannot see the difference. Fewer triangles for nothing.
src.t.eblf30: Shadows: none, a soft dark blob under things, or a proper shadow map, which draws the whole scene a second time from the light.
src.t.78pcsr: Anti-aliasing: shading every pixel several times at the edges so staircases look smooth. Two times or four times as many samples.
src.t.1ec0n2d: sha1 turns any bytes into a short fingerprint. Change one letter of the file and the fingerprint is completely different.
src.t.qafnkr: The object goes on disk under its id. Ask for the id later, get the same bytes back.
src.t.1s1z5be: A counter hands out the next free number. It does not care what is inside, so two copies of a file get two numbers.
src.t.3b8tpx: content is the bytes of the file, exactly. An object’s id should depend on nothing else.
src.t.3cwk92: lcs, the longest common subsequence: the most lines, in order, that both versions have. Everything outside it is what changed.
src.t.17oh7t5: edits walks both files along the common lines and writes down what is added and what is removed in between.
src.t.zb0e8i: zip puts line one next to line one, line two next to line two. Insert one line at the top and every pair after it is out of step.
src.t.1s95tvv: same and change are the two things this version knows: the pair matches, or the pair is a change.
src.t.75lz32: Lines only in the old file are removed, lines only in the new file are added. Where they were, and in what order, it does not ask.
src.t.1vghlzk: base is the common ancestor: the last version both branches started from. Without it you cannot tell who changed what.
src.t.1tmfi6w: ours is the branch we merge into, theirs the one we merge in. Each is compared with base to see what that side really changed.
src.t.dqogu5: combine takes both lists of changes. Different places: apply both. The same place, differently: a conflict, and a human decides.
src.t.1eaovwe: The window: how many earlier files git tries as a base for a delta. A wider window finds better bases and takes longer to repack.
src.t.6yxz2h: depth is the longest chain of deltas. The deeper, the smaller the pack, and the more steps to rebuild an old file.
src.t.q0jee0: Runners are the machines that run the tests. Every push waits in line for a free one, and every runner is on the bill.
src.t.n6txcz: The dependency cache: the libraries are downloaded once and kept. A job that does not download everything again finishes in half the time.
src.t.10gdlav: When a test fails by itself (a flaky one) the runner tries it again. Without retries a good change shows a red cross for no reason.
src.t.1pyclsw: update_curr runs all the time: it looks at how long the running task has been on the CPU and writes that on its clock.
src.t.12uki2n: The run queue of the fair scheduler: everyone who is ready to run and waiting for a turn on this CPU.
src.t.4mmv16: delta_exec is the time the task just ran, since we last looked. A few microseconds, added up thousands of times a second.
src.t.fnnouk: vruntime, virtual runtime: a clock per task that says how much CPU it has had, corrected for its priority. The task with the smallest one is the one most owed a turn.
src.t.g76aex: The weight of a nice 0 task, 1024. A heavier task counts as less time for its clock, a lighter one as more.
src.t.1vcfc58: The weight comes from the nice value: each nice step is about 25 percent more or less CPU. Nice -5 is about 3121, nice 19 is 15.
src.t.1k1chds: exec_start is when we last looked at the clock. The difference with the clock now is how long the task ran in between.
src.t.156rqzq: Called whenever a slice ends or a task blocks: who gets the CPU next? Everything about fairness is decided in these few lines.
src.t.jeo2fi: The run queue is a red-black tree sorted by vruntime. The leftmost node, the smallest, is kept in a cache, so finding it costs nothing.
src.t.cykzy: A plain list: the first in line goes next, then goes to the back. Fair in turns, and blind to priorities and to who just woke up.
src.t.1bxnvpl: The highest priority always wins. As long as one important task is runnable, the unimportant ones never get a turn at all.
src.t.r276mr: The lock that guards the list of every task in the system. top, ps and /proc read it all the time, fork and exit change it.
src.t.2vf27e: RCU, read-copy-update: readers walk the list without waiting for anyone. A writer makes a new copy and waits until the old readers are gone.
src.t.2rcz8y: A spinlock: whoever waits just keeps asking, burning its CPU, with interrupts off. Fine for a few instructions, bad for a walk through 400 tasks.
src.t.1fy734g: A mutex puts the waiter to sleep. Sleeping is forbidden in places like the OOM killer or an interrupt, where there is nobody to wake us up.
src.t.3tg17f: Walks the list of every process on the machine, one after the other.
src.t.1sdczhn: show_task prints one line for one process, the way top does: pid, name, cpu, state.
src.t.1e4w1g: The target latency: the period in which every runnable task should get a turn. A short period feels snappy; a long one wastes less time switching.
src.t.pij2hw: The minimum slice. However many tasks are waiting, none is kicked off the CPU sooner than this. Tiny slices mean the CPU is mostly changing seats.
src.t.11dbhzx: When a task wakes up with much less vruntime than the running one, it may push in at once instead of waiting for the slice to end. That is what keeps vim snappy.
src.t.1juxsn7: A task that slept returns with a little bonus on its clock, so it gets served first. Without it, waking up means joining the back of the queue.
src.t.1jjflcl: Losers are transactions that never wrote their commit record. Their changes, even those that reached the disk, are taken back.
src.t.1796zvw: Selectivity is the share of the table a condition matches, estimated from statistics. One row in a hundred thousand is very selective.
src.t.1ay61p8: The cost of reading one page when the pages are read in order. The disk loves it: one long stretch.
src.t.1249eds: The cost of reading one page from a random place: about four times a sequential page.
src.t.1jep3uj: The cost of looking at one row in memory. Tiny, but a hundred thousand of them add up.
src.t.1pzzmz1: Two ways to find rows: walk the index to the matches, or read the whole table in order and check each row.
src.t.1jpibpt: The planner’s knowledge of the table: how many rows and pages, how values are spread, how deep the index is.
src.t.o9gyk7: The buffer pool: pages kept in memory so the disk is asked less. More is faster, until the machine runs out of RAM and starts swapping.
src.t.dg543g: Bytes per page. Bigger pages mean a shallower index, but every read drags in more rows you did not want.
src.t.266w86: How often all the dirty pages are written out. Frequent checkpoints make crash recovery short, but keep the disk busy.
src.t.1yqziyz: Whether the primary waits for the replica to have the change before saying “committed”. sync: safe and slower. async: fast, and a moment behind.
src.t.1bhbib0: Where read queries go: only the primary, or spread across the replicas. More capacity, but a replica can be a moment out of date.
src.t.p4sh2e: Listen up. Children love 8-bit. Sixteen is double that, so we will make them *twice* as happy.
src.t.u9utia: It is called *TeaBit*. A tea glass called Sam jumps over bugs and collects sugar cubes. On a cartridge. With a physical box. Nostalgia sells.
src.t.1liwpfh: The console has, I am told, sixteen colours, two hundred and fifty-six tiles and… a very small processor. Make it look like a million colours. Quickly.
src.t.1pztv4t: Everything on a console is a budget, my friends. Colours, tiles, sprites per line, cycles per frame, bytes in the chip. Spend one and you pay for it somewhere else.
src.t.11i899q: I can do the collision. Floors are easy. What could go wrong?
src.t.1tenlnb: Open the 📋 board on a laptop. Take tasks yourself, or ask a friend to do them.
src.t.afli38: You do not pick sixteen colours by hand. You let the computer try: scatter sixteen points among all the colours, let every pixel join its nearest point, then move each point to the middle of its group. Again. And again.
src.t.1vqwxe1: It is called *k-means*. Like me sorting the office into sugar-takers: first guess is bad, but each round people move to the group that suits them and the groups settle.
src.t.tmspu: Past sixteen the console just throws colours away. Run it for too few rounds and the groups never settle.
src.t.1711onq: The console draws the background from little 8 by 8 squares. The map says “tile 17 here, tile 4 there”. A big meadow is one tile used a hundred times.
src.t.eo48bb: The chip remembers 256 different squares. Merge exact copies, and mirror images too, since the chip can flip a tile for free. Merge squares that are *nearly* the same and you save more, but smear the picture.
src.t.2fzc75: Each frame we move him and ask “is he inside a floor now?”. If he moved twelve pixels and the plank is two, he can be above it one frame and below it the next, and at no moment inside it.
src.t.1udl9p0: It is called *tunnelling*. Like asking a courier whether he is at the door at exactly noon, when he came at 11:59 and left at 12:01. A *swept* test follows the whole trip.
src.t.v3zoq8: The picture chip paints the screen one row at a time, like me pouring one row of glasses on the tray. It only has hands for eight sprites per row. The ninth is simply not drawn.
src.t.1hqfonp: If it is always the same sprite, it disappears for good. So games rotate who loses. Everyone blinks a little instead of one of us vanishing.
src.t.1ocetk5: The television wants a new picture sixty times a second. The processor does about 1.79 million steps a second, so each picture gets 29,830 steps. Run over, and the game waits for the next picture: it plays slower.
src.t.4a09vj: So every job gets a price. Reading the pad is cheap. A square root per bug is not. Choose what is worth its steps.
src.t.1ma36dv: The wave is up for a slice of each cycle. A thin slice sounds nasal, half and half sounds hollow, a quarter is the sweet spot for tunes.
src.t.qjfsio: Add the channels together and the sum can be louder than the speaker takes. It clips: crunch. Divide them, or squash them with a gentle mixer.
src.t.168brll: Art in, cartridge out. Sixteen colours, 256 tiles, eight sprites a line, 29,830 cycles a frame. Everything else is cosmetic. I have a call.
src.t.wrlgri: The artist painted in every colour she could find. The console cannot show most of them, so the art has to be squeezed.
src.t.fwmt9n: K-means finds the sixteen colours that lose the least: drop k points in colour space, let every pixel join its nearest, move each point to the middle of its group, repeat.
src.t.5licx0: The level is cut into 8 by 8 squares. Identical ones are stored once and the map holds only tile numbers. The console remembers 256 different squares and not one more.
src.t.29akmk: Sam falls, lands, jumps. If a frame’s move is longer than the floor is thick, a naive test jumps straight over it: tunnelling. A swept test walks the whole move.
src.t.ca7u6e: The picture chip draws sprites row by row and gives up after eight on a row. A swarm near Sam means somebody gets dropped. Rotating who makes it flicker instead of vanish.
src.t.17bhx5s: Square waves with different widths, a triangle for the bass and noise for drums. The channels are summed, and a sum can go past what the speaker takes.
src.t.14cxo5j: The CPU has about thirty thousand cycles before the TV wants the next picture. Spend more and the game simply plays slower. So each job gets a rate.
src.t.7h757y: Code, music, map and graphics must all fit in the ROM chip. Bigger chips cost real money. Compression is free ROM but costs time.
src.t.wimcjp: A child, a sofa and a television. The only customers who forgive nothing.
src.t.rslbt1: Demo time. Show me TeaBit. And it better not crash.
src.t.1n2hud6: TeaBit. Sugar Cube Sam, a tea glass with legs, on a cartridge. Sixteen colours, 256 tiles, zero excuses.
src.t.80hiq1: I played it on the toilet for an hour. That is the highest compliment I know.
src.t.13lk3c3: My nephew says the floor is “optional” and the sky is “broken”. Fix the floor.
src.t.9tspxy: Listen up. Open world. *Everyone* wants an open world. Players want to go anywhere. Right now they can go to the kitchen.
src.t.yjvpoe: It is called *Grand Tea Delivery*. You drive a tea van around a whole city and deliver tea. That is the game. The city is *very* large. And no loading screens. I hate screens.
src.t.1gq8srx: It must have crowds. Traffic. Draw distance to the horizon. Ray tracing. And it must run at sixty frames on the console I bought for the meeting room.
src.t.q722y1: Everything big in a game is a trick. The city is not there until you are close, far things are painted cheap, and time itself is cut into slices. Spend where the player looks.
src.t.nyzre9: I can do the routing maths. Someone take the physics loop?
src.t.8ur5d6: The same way I serve a ten-floor building from one tray: only the floors near me are in my head. The city lives on disk in chunks, and only the ones around the van are loaded.
src.t.1tmt3d7: Drive on, and the ones behind are dropped, the ones ahead come in. Too small a window and buildings pop up in front of you. Too big and the memory is gone.
src.t.ou88ci: A building close to you needs windows and doors. The same building a kilometre away is four pixels: a plain box will do. So every building has several versions and we pick by distance.
src.t.1xvbhzy: Same with the crowd. Nobody counts the pedestrians a street away, so they are cheap.
src.t.1706lmb: You can: that is Dijkstra, and it is always right. But thirty taxis, every few seconds, each looking at the whole city. The frame is gone.
src.t.jaho5d: *A-star* adds a guess of what is left, a straight line at the fastest speed. As long as the guess is never too pessimistic, you still get the best route, but you look mostly toward the goal.
src.t.1wijt4a: Look only at the guess and you rush at the river like a pigeon at a window. Quick, and not always clever.
src.t.w2afa4: A long frame, a fast van, a thin fence. If we move the van by the whole long frame in one go, it can start on one side and land on the other and never be “in” the fence.
src.t.1ustex9: The cure: slice time. Keep an *accumulator* of time owed and spend it in equal little steps. A long frame is just several steps. And every run gives the same result.
src.t.1hiolbc: Spend only one step per frame and the game plays in slow motion on a slow day. Careful with that one.
src.t.aiias4: A list of rules for a pedestrian: the first one whose condition is true is what he does. Van coming, jump aside. Late for work, run. Thirsty, queue for tea. Otherwise, wander.
src.t.ryodry: Order is everything. Put “wander” first and it is always true, so nobody ever jumps aside. Put “stand and stare” before it and you get pedestrians in hedges. Comedy, but not what we want.
src.t.logsjl: Sixty frames a second leaves sixteen and a bit milliseconds for everything: every building drawn, every pedestrian thought about, every car routed.
src.t.1mq26x9: The boss wants everything: a far horizon, a big crowd, a shiny picture. Each is a few milliseconds, and the bill is paid by the frame rate. Ray tracing nearly doubles it. I would not mention that to him yet.
src.t.waxz2b: A whole city, no loading screens. Stream it, simplify it, route it, step it. Every box is on the sheet. I have a call.
src.t.tzcesu: The whole of Çay City, on disk, cut into chunks. It is far bigger than the console’s memory.
src.t.ncjz51: Keeps a window of chunks around the van: load ahead, drop behind. A window too small and buildings pop in; too big and the memory is gone.
src.t.1cd89lf: Near buildings get windows and doors, far ones a plain box. Drawing everything in full detail would take longer than a frame.
src.t.1hmuxax: Everything above adds up to milliseconds per frame. Over 16.7 and the game is no longer sixty frames a second.
src.t.icxn4w: Cars find routes by best-first search. Add the cost so far to an honest guess of what is left, and you get the best route looking at few junctions.
src.t.mxk4v1: Each pedestrian checks its rules top to bottom and does the first thing that applies. Put “jump aside” last and you get pedestrians in hedges.
src.t.whdbwo: Real frames come at uneven times; physics wants a steady beat. An accumulator turns a long frame into several fixed steps, so a fast van cannot skip a thin fence.
src.t.114711y: Players send crash reports. Each belongs to one part of the engine, or to a graphics driver, or is a copy of another. Sending it to the wrong person wastes a week.
src.t.o24kfh: The last choice is the picture: resolution, target frame rate, and whether to trace rays. Bigger pictures cost frame time.
src.t.ksacs: Someone who wants to drive a van full of tea in a straight line into a river, at 60 frames a second.
src.t.63ttk4: Demo time. Show me Grand Tea Delivery. And it better not crash.
src.t.8twjon: Grand Tea Delivery. Drive a tea van around a whole city. Nobody loads. Nothing pops in. Everything is also on fire (optional).
src.t.12447pv: I drove for an hour and never once saw a loading screen. I did see a pedestrian in a hedge. Marketing says that is “emergent”.
src.t.d1bdbx: The van drove into a river that was also a fence. The pedestrians stared at me. I am leaving them a one-star review.
src.t.aaykmy: Listen up. Everyone is making films. The big studios have render farms the size of Kadıköy. We have a garage and a dream.
src.t.1vbmbvn: Two ways. The painter: sort the triangles by distance and draw the far ones first, like the stage painters at the theatre. Falls over when they cross, like our sugar cube in the ball.
src.t.um7bqc: The z-buffer: a notebook with a number for every pixel, the nearest depth so far. Whoever is nearer, wins. It does not care about the order. Every GPU does this.
src.t.1ne7pa9: Not drawing what nobody sees. Objects behind you, outside the camera’s pyramid: skip them whole, with one cheap test on a bounding sphere.
src.t.1ydljdb: And back faces: a triangle seen from behind is the inside of something solid. Which side is the front is a rule you pick, the winding: counter-clockwise. Get it backwards and you see the insides.
src.t.7ndb2e: Because frames are different lengths, and small errors add up differently. A ball dropped at 30 frames a second lands slightly elsewhere than at 144. Two players, two different games.
src.t.lpctzv: So: spend the real time in equal chunks of a sixtieth of a second, keep the leftover for the next frame, and tell the renderer how much is left over so it can draw in between.
src.t.878ehs: Entities are just numbers, like table numbers in the tea house. Components are the data on the table: position, speed, colour. Systems are the waiters: one does all the positions, one does all the drawing.
src.t.1xe3ezw: They go round in a fixed order each frame. If the drawing waiter goes before the moving waiter, every picture is one frame old, and the player feels the controls are sticky.
src.t.1cd45hn: Sixty frames a second is a sixtieth of a second each: sixteen and two-thirds milliseconds. The game takes a couple, the vertices one, and the pixels most of the rest.
src.t.1b6xmo3: Pixels multiply: more resolution, shadow maps, anti-aliasing. So that is where you save. Nobody notices 75 percent of the pixels. Everyone notices a stutter.
src.t.1gt73wn: Matrix, divide, cull, rasterise, and do it sixty times a second. Seven boxes. The loop is the important one. I have a meeting.
src.t.9s6x6y: The loop decides how game time passes. Updating in fixed steps keeps the game the same on a slow laptop and a fast one.
src.t.jurlyz: Entities are just numbers; components hold the data; systems are loops over them. They run in a fixed order, and swapping two makes the data a frame old.
src.t.ywjsr1: The garage and eighty-odd tea glasses, cubes and pyramids. Each has a mesh, a model matrix and a bounding sphere.
src.t.ug66sn: Do not draw what cannot be seen: objects outside the camera’s pyramid, and triangles facing away.
src.t.p1vii5: Three matrices multiplied into one: model, view, projection. The order matters, and it reads right to left.
src.t.8tzmdp: The divide by w is where perspective happens. Far things have a big w and shrink.
src.t.9m90te: For each triangle, find the pixels it covers and keep the nearest surface per pixel with a z-buffer.
src.t.nu2z6u: At sixty frames a second a frame has 16.7 milliseconds. Pixels cost the most, so resolution, shadows and anti-aliasing are where you save.
src.t.1nzui2t: The picture. Drag to orbit: every pixel was drawn by the team’s renderer.
src.t.1i7h5rq: Demo time. Show me Kıvılcım. And it better not crash.
src.t.spsela: Kıvılcım. A software 3D engine for the tea-garage game. 60 frames a second, or the boss starts counting.
src.t.8oc6ge: I orbited the tea glass for ten minutes. My cousin asks if the engine can do cars.
src.t.ug5rjp: Rıza orbited it and felt ill. He asked for a tea. A flat one.
src.t.1uq18n: Everyone keeps their code in a place with an octopus-cat. We keep ours in a USB stick. This changes. *Today.*
src.t.jijzat: It’s called *GitHan*. A han is a caravanserai: travellers rest, camels get water. Here the travellers are commits. Legal says it’s original. Legal is my cousin’s camel.
src.t.e1ebd9: It has a file tree, a history, a diff and a big green MERGE button. I press the button, the code merges. If something disappears, it was not important.
src.t.uz6axx: It is not important until it is *your* sugar cap that disappears. Boss, a merge button that eats work is a shredder with a nice colour.
src.t.1b1anay: And remember: git never stores the same file twice. It names things by what is inside them. I do the same with my tea glasses: no two on the tray have the same name, no glass is washed twice.
src.t.1itwqfd: I will do the merge. And I did not force-push to main last night, whatever the log says.
src.t.mxufbj: Open the 📋 board. The object store, the diff and the push rules do not need each other. The merge needs the diff.
src.t.lgff6i: Look at my tea tray. If I name every glass by what is in it, “Turkish tea, two sugars”, then two identical glasses are *the same glass*. I only have to wash one.
src.t.12iskhl: Git makes a fingerprint of the bytes, a *hash*, and uses it as the name. The same file twice is one object. Move a file, nothing new. And if a byte rots on the disk, the name no longer matches, and everybody knows.
src.t.u991dk: Two guest lists, before and after the party. You do not compare name one with name one, or one latecomer at the top makes the whole list look different.
src.t.1i2dq0k: You find the *longest common subsequence*: the most people, in order, who are on both lists. Everyone outside it arrived or left. That is a diff.
src.t.epbbrm: The bag-of-lines idea is worse: the guest who moved from table three to table five is invisible, and the list will not rebuild the party.
src.t.1gh6y9n: Two cooks get the same recipe. One writes “steep 5 minutes”, the other “steep 4”. Looking at their two versions you only see they differ.
src.t.smozyo: Put the *original* beside them and it is clear: the first one changed the steeping time, the second changed the sugar. Change by one cook only: take it. Same line changed by both, differently: a conflict, and a human with a tea decides.
src.t.1ldqhlm: A merge that always takes the incoming file is a fast way to lose someone’s Friday.
src.t.1c5h3hx: Imagine the menu, rewritten every week with three changes. You do not keep a full copy of every menu. You keep the first and a note for each week: “line four is new”.
src.t.yhycpw: It’s called *Pixelçay*. The hero is Bardak, a tea glass. He hops three times and the audience weeps. Can the tears be AI?
src.t.1b5b60w: Sixty seconds, fourteen hundred and forty frames, premiere at six. Make it look expensive. Pay as little as possible.
src.t.12mnn9y: Tea, anyone? Tip: light adds up in *linear* numbers and screens speak in *gamma*. Mix them up and Bardak looks like he was left on the stove.
src.t.1jbawt5: I’ll do the shaders. I watched a video once.
src.t.ond68o: Because nothing in life starts or stops in an instant. A glass thrown up slows down at the top, speeds up when it falls. Straight lines change speed in one frame, and the eye sees it.
src.t.80hd0n: So the animators put little handles on each key. Flat at the top of the hop means slow there. And keep the handles short, or the curve swings right through the floor.
src.t.1p69g9n: Bardak’s mesh is a skin; inside are bones. Each bit of skin has weights: “sixty percent follow the foot, forty the rim”. It goes where the weighted average of the bones takes it.
src.t.70cib7: Weighted average only works when the weights sum to one. Sum to two, and the skin goes twice as far as it should. Like asking me for a tea and a half and getting the whole tray.
src.t.fnsfn6: Backwards. From the camera, through each pixel, you follow a ray until it hits something, then bounce it somewhere random and see if it finds the lamp. Do it a few hundred times per pixel and average.
src.t.6njmbq: Few samples means grain: each pixel only heard two rumours. Four times more samples halves the grain. Four times the work for half the grain: that is the bargain.
src.t.ajuf2r: Screens do not show numbers evenly: they are squeezed so that dark shades get more room, because your eye is fussy about darks. Light itself adds up evenly, though.
src.t.h2z9m1: So: decode the textures to linear, do the light maths, and encode with sRGB only at the very end. Skip the encode and it is dark. Skip the decode and the glass looks washed out.
src.t.1kvievs: A patch that reflects exactly eighteen percent of the light. Every set has one. In linear that is 0.18, which on a correct screen reads 118 out of 255. If your grey card says something else, your whole pipeline is lying.
src.t.42aitq: A surface cannot send back more light than it gets. Plain old Blinn-Phong adds the glint on top, like pouring a second tea into an already full glass: it spills. The energy-conserving version takes the glint out of what is left for the colour, and makes a tight glint stronger, a wide one weaker.
src.t.1qfj1az: Many machines, each some frames. The trick is the splash scene: it costs more than twice a normal frame. Give each machine a fixed block and two of them get the splash, and everyone waits for them.
src.t.1itqmm5: A shared queue gives the next frame to whoever is free. And you pay by the minute, so idle nodes are lit cigarettes. Spot machines are a third of the price, but may be taken back mid-frame.
src.t.15tg74l: Each stage eats what the one before made. You cannot skin a pose nobody evaluated. And you must tone-map and denoise while the numbers are still light, in linear, then do the sRGB encode last. Encode early and you smooth and squash the wrong numbers.
src.t.1kmoghs: Curves move the rig, the rig moves the mesh, the tracer lights it, the farm does it 1,440 times. Eight boxes. Premiere is at six.
src.t.1dre4en: The animators set a few keys: here Bardak is on the floor, here he is at the top. The computer fills in every frame between them with a curve.
src.t.1aslhgl: The rig is a skeleton inside the glass. Skinning says how strongly each bone pulls each vertex. The weights must add up to one, or vertices fly away.
src.t.cshhbv: For each frame: evaluate the curves, move the mesh, and build a structure so rays can find what they hit quickly. Order matters.
src.t.dul3ux: A shader says what colour a point is, given the light and where you look from. Glass needs a glint, but a glint must not be extra light.
src.t.11pphda: The tracer shoots light paths backwards from the camera, bounces them around and averages. More samples, less grain, more minutes.
src.t.53jr4r: Light adds up in linear numbers but screens expect encoded ones. Do the maths in linear, then encode at the very end.
src.t.1xdx29n: The output: one picture per frame. A sixty-second trailer is fourteen hundred and forty of them.
src.t.1eceo7s: Many machines each render some frames. You choose how many, how frames are handed out, and whether to rent cheap machines that may be taken back.
src.t.o6gs64: Where the boss watches it. Every pixel in there was computed from the team’s choices.
src.t.2yrytn: Demo time. Show me Pixelçay. And it better not crash.
src.t.a10a5f: Pixelçay. A tea glass learns to hop. 1,440 frames of ray-traced feelings, rendered before the premiere.
src.t.f6kl72: I watched it twice. Bardak is moving. My cousin wants the glass’s autograph.
src.t.18s73x4: Rıza watched it and asked if the glass was on fire. It was not, Rıza. It was “artistic”.
src.t.1qcw0jm: Listen up. Games make more money than films and music together. I read it on a mug. We are making a *game engine*.
src.t.zsyf6w: It’s called *Kıvılcım*. It does 3D. It does sixty frames a second. I want to be able to spin a tea glass with the mouse and not be sick.
src.t.fy0p9f: No Unreal, no Unity, no GPU. It runs on a laptop that I bought in 2014. Can we put blockchain in the physics?
src.t.10tubx8: Tea, anyone? Tip: matrices are not like numbers. Three times two is two times three; a matrix times another matrix is *not*. Mind the order.
src.t.4pg57j: I’ll take the loop. I’ve played a lot of games.
src.t.up43i: Moving it. A matrix is a recipe for “turn, stretch and shift” in one go. Model: place the glass in the garage. View: stand where the camera stands. Projection: squeeze it through the lens.
src.t.wkcld9: And the order matters, like in my kitchen: sugar then tea is not tea then sugar. Read right to left: P times V times M means M happens first.
src.t.11s4eqp: The projection matrix does not make them small. It keeps the distance in a fourth number, w. The *divide* by w does the shrinking: the farther, the bigger the w, the smaller the picture.
src.t.1ex9oxl: Skip the divide and everything is the same size, like a floor plan. Divide by the wrong number and the depths are all one, and nothing knows what is in front.
src.t.nxg9wo: To read last month’s menu you start from the first and follow the notes. Long chains are tiny and slow to follow, short chains are bigger and quick. The *window* is how many menus you look through to find a good one to compare with.
src.t.3gv9rl: Sixty-four people send a parcel at four o’clock. Three counters open. Everybody waits. A *cache* is like keeping the stamps at the counter: every parcel goes in half the time.
src.t.1aw6qj5: And one test in seven is *flaky*, it fails sometimes for no reason, like my samovar on humid days. With a retry the runner tries again and the good build stays green. Without it someone gets a red cross and writes an angry message.
src.t.pz2ksx: The doorman of a tea house knows three answers: come in, wait here while I ask the owner, or not today. A typo fix with a green check: come in. A 3 a.m. hotfix: wait, call the one who is awake.
src.t.suqawx: Force-pushes, secret keys, a four-hundred-megabyte video of the boss: not today. And “I am the boss” is not a review. The boss is the person who most needs one.
src.t.1ljyfra: Push goes in, objects get stored, merges come out. A rule at the door, a queue at the back. Eight boxes. I have a tunnel to catch.
src.t.erhay2: Four friends, forty branches and one deadline. They push their work here and pull everybody else’s.
src.t.5jta79: A doorman for the main branch. Typo fix with a green check: in. Force-push, a secret key or a 400 MB video: not today.
src.t.n7i73v: Everything is stored under the fingerprint of its content. Same file twice, stored once. Change a byte and the id changes, so damage cannot hide.
src.t.1qyseqa: Old versions of a file are stored as the small difference from another version. The disk bill shrinks; reading gets a few steps longer.
src.t.kul60b: Finds what changed between two versions by keeping the longest run of lines they share. A good diff is short and can be applied.
src.t.x2f9r9: Compares each branch with the common ancestor. What only one side changed goes in; where both changed the same lines, it asks a human.
src.t.1vnzfji: The website: file tree, history graph, diffs and the big merge button. It shows exactly what the boxes above compute.
src.t.kjg1ev: Machines that run the tests on every push. Too few and everyone waits in a queue; too many and the bill grows.
src.t.w71ik7: Demo time. Show me GitHan. And it better not crash.
src.t.1vo9qx2: GitHan. Where code stays the night. Branches, pull requests and a very opinionated merge button.
src.t.dmfgaj: I pressed the green button forty times. Nothing vanished. Ece is crying, but with joy.
src.t.1x532qp: I merged Kaan’s branch and my own commit disappeared. I do not know which of us was deleted.
src.t.1nwm1yy: Computers do many things at once. This is a lie. They do *one* thing, very fast, and hope you do not look. I want the part that decides what.
src.t.12plb8v: It’s called *Linüks*. Like the other one, but with an umlaut. We put it in the kernel. I have heard the kernel is where the popcorn is.
src.t.ddiqh: It must be *completely fair*. Except to my video, which comes first. And my editor. And nobody touches the miner. I mean, the *thing* in the corner. It is mine. It is not mine.
src.t.j66wns: The miner is minerd, pid 4242, nice zero, and it has been eating a third of the CPU since March. We will *renice* it to 19 once the scheduler respects nice.
src.t.18hj8ip: Fair means this: everyone has a ticket clock. The clock runs slower for important people. Whoever is furthest behind gets served. I do this with the tea queue and nobody has complained since 2019.
src.t.180wx1s: There is a maintainer. Gunnar Nakken. I read the list. He once replied to a patch with only the word “no”. Then he replied “no” to that.
src.t.351k6j: Open the 📋 board. The clock, the queue and the lock are three separate jobs. The timeslice needs the first two; the patch and the boot come last.
src.t.b7jzfn: One tea machine, forty thirsty people. The scheduler is the person who decides whose glass is filled next, and for how long, so everyone thinks they are being served at the same time.
src.t.1fwpx91: The turn is short, a few milliseconds. If it is too short I spend all day walking between glasses; too long and the one who only wants a sip waits at the back.
src.t.ho663a: Each guest has a card: how many glasses I have had. I serve whoever has the *least*. That is fair, and it is also what vruntime is: a clock of CPU time received.
src.t.8hcx7w: But the boss pays for *three* glasses to everyone’s one. So his card fills slower: each glass counts for a third. The clock runs at one over the weight. That is what nice does: nice -5 is a weight of about 3000, nice 19 only 15.
src.t.1526vwy: Forget the division and everyone’s card fills at the same speed, and the miner you wanted to hide at nice 19 has as many glasses as the boss.
src.t.1d0uwv2: The cards are kept in a sorted tree, like pigeonholes: the smallest number is always in the leftmost hole, and the kernel keeps a finger on it. Taking the next one costs nothing. Putting a card back costs a few steps down the tree.
src.t.1nx5dzc: The line of people in order of arrival is the wrong tool. And “highest priority always first” is worse: the important ones eat all the tea and the backup waits until Tuesday. Forever.
src.t.eh23pt: Every time I move to another glass I lose a moment: the tray, the spoon, the lemon. In a CPU that is the cache going cold, and it costs about as much as a good chunk of a millisecond.
src.t.r23ar6: So there is a *target latency*, everybody gets a turn within it, and a *minimum granularity*, no turn is shorter than this, however many are waiting. The right numbers are a compromise between a snappy vim and a fast compile.
src.t.gb47j3: A sleeper wakes up with a card that has very few glasses on it, because it slept while others drank. With *wakeup preemption* the kernel notices: “this one is far behind” and serves it right away, instead of letting the compile finish its slice.
src.t.12fxmok: But the kernel itself must let go. With *none* preemption a task in a system call cannot be interrupted at all. *Voluntary* adds polite places to stop. *Full* lets almost anything be interrupted, and costs a little speed. And HZ is how often the metronome ticks.
src.t.1olkgze: Reading the list of all tasks. A spinlock is a door with one key: the others stand outside and ask “is it free yet?” until they are dizzy. A mutex sends them to sleep in the armchair, but some people, like the OOM killer, are not allowed to sit down.
src.t.12hglme: *RCU* is a notice board. Readers just read it, all at once. The writer pins a new notice, waits until everyone who read the old one has gone home, then takes the old one down. Perfect when there are many readers and few writers: our case exactly.
src.t.1p66ze7: It travels by mail, plain text, to the person in charge of that part. Subject with the part’s name in front. Then *why*, because the code already shows the what. Then proof it works. Then your signature that the work is yours.
src.t.hx2cxi: Gunnar Nakken, who looks after the scheduler, answers many patches with one word. It is “NAK”. The trick is to send him nothing he can say it about.
src.t.xi9q31: Tasks want the CPU. The clock says who had it. The tree says who is next. Eight boxes, one CPU. I have a plane.
src.t.17w3etm: The garage workload. Some tasks sleep and wake in tiny bursts, some never stop. The scheduler must serve both without anyone noticing.
src.t.le1zww: The kernel’s metronome. Each tick it checks whether the running task has had enough. A slow metronome means slow decisions.
src.t.2t3496: Every task has a clock of how much CPU it has had, scaled by its weight. Heavier tasks age slower, so they come up more often.
src.t.1tzqec7: A tree of everyone who is ready, sorted by their clock. The leftmost, the one furthest behind, goes next.
src.t.1ckm3wd: How long a turn lasts: the period is shared by everyone who is ready, but never below a minimum. Short turns are snappy, long ones waste less on switching.
src.t.3l002g: top and /proc walk the list of every task; fork and exit change it. The lock decides if eight CPUs can read at once.
src.t.1a167wo: A virtual machine that runs your scheduler for real. Start a compile, renice the miner, watch the numbers.
src.t.1228sjy: Kernel changes are mailed as plain text to the maintainer. He reads the why, the numbers and the sign-off, and answers “NAK” very quickly.
src.t.cwlbt3: Demo time. Show me Linüks. And it better not crash.
src.t.16b8esb: Linüks. The part of the kernel that decides whose turn it is. Completely fair. Mostly.
src.t.mghk50: I started a compile, a video and I think a miner. Nothing stuttered. Gunnar replied “applied”. I have never seen a happier word.
src.t.z14x2u: My editor lags. Gunnar replied with the letters N, A, K. I do not know what they mean but they sound final.
src.t.104oxya: Payments. Everyone has them. *We* take money by hand, from Rıza, in a pocket. That ends today.
src.t.xgmvzl: It’s called *Stripey*. Like the other one, with a stripe. Legal says it’s fine. Legal is still my cousin.
src.t.wshq00: People tap Pay, money arrives. I want it on the blockchain. No? Then at least on the cloud. And nobody pays twice, except me, to myself.
src.t.1watnq6: Tea, anyone? Tip: a computer cannot hold 0.1 exactly, and a phone *will* ask twice. Everything about money is about those two facts.
src.t.8pxbqo: I’ll take the fraud model. Someone do the money type, the ledger, the bank bits?
src.t.hxemmy: Because a computer counts in twos, not tens. 0.1 has no exact form, like one third has none in decimals. Add 0.1 and 0.2 and you get 0.30000000000000004.
src.t.1owt6w: So we count *kuruş*, whole numbers: 1250 for twelve lira fifty. Integers are exact. Round once, on purpose, where a percentage needs it. The way I count sugar cubes, never half a cube.
src.t.1fxosfh: A ledger is the notebook of who has what. Double entry: every movement is written twice, once where the money left and once where it arrived.
src.t.q4zva7: Take a hundred from the customer, give ninety-seven to the shop, three to us. Minus a hundred, plus ninety-seven, plus three: zero. Always zero. If the sum is not zero, a bug is hiding, and you *know* it. With one entry, money just appears, and nobody notices.
src.t.l66n24: The phone makes up a ticket number for each purchase and sends it with every try. You write the ticket and the answer in your notebook. A second request with the same ticket? You read the answer back. You do not charge again.
src.t.1rnflpp: Like my queue ticket for tea: shout the same number twice and you get one glass. Guessing duplicates by amount is worse: two friends ordering the same tea would be refused.
src.t.owgm8: When the bank is down, asking every second is like four hundred people knocking on a door at once. It cannot open. When it finally wakes up, the crowd knocks it over again.
src.t.2gmrkb: So wait one second, then two, then four. And add *jitter*: a random bit, so nobody comes back at the same moment. Backoff is politeness. Jitter is not being in a queue with your friends.
src.t.183eb7r: It adds up evidence. Night-time? A card ten minutes old? Another country? The wrong CVC? Each signal pushes a score up or down, and the model learned the weights from old payments, labelled fraud or fine.
src.t.19z8nsj: It is *logistic regression*: weights times signals, squashed into nought to one. Then you pick a line. Block above it, let through below. Where you put the line is a business choice.
src.t.zbg8fx: High line: few angry customers, more thieves. Low line: no thieves, and Mimar Arda cannot buy a simit on holiday. A code from the bank in the grey zone helps. The honest type it, thieves do not have the phone.
src.t.rnq2dl: Every night the bank sends a list of what it thinks happened. You hold it next to your own list, line by line. Equal lines cancel.
src.t.b606v4: Some differences are only timing, a payment the bank settles tomorrow. Leave those. The rest, an extra kuruş, a double charge, a chargeback, a person must look at. It is closing time at the tea house: count the till against the notebook.
src.t.rjp5f6: Pay, check, charge, write down, compare with the bank. Eight boxes. Money moves left to right. The bug moves faster.
src.t.1r3rdgp: The customer taps Pay. If the Wi-Fi hiccups after the bank said yes, the phone does not know, and asks again.
src.t.o7ep8r: The front door. It looks the key up first: seen this one before? Then it returns the old answer instead of charging again.
src.t.1p72g5x: A small model reads six signals about the payment and gives a risk score. Above the threshold the payment is blocked.
src.t.1auctak: The bank. It is not always up, and it does not like being shouted at: too many requests at once and it falls over again.
src.t.ad0fjz: How the code stores an amount. Whole kuruş as integers are exact; decimals are not.
src.t.f46ufs: The truth about who has what. Every movement leaves one account and arrives at another, written together, so the sum is always zero.
src.t.1qce8xa: Every night the bank sends a statement. We compare it with the ledger line by line, and a person looks at the lines that differ.
src.t.qkgpj1: What the boss watches: how much came in, how many were declined, and whether the books add up.
src.t.7vl1vg: I delivered tea to the whole city and nobody noticed a single loading screen. Magnificent. I will call it a franchise.
src.t.mgn1pi: The city is big, the tea arrives. A building appeared in front of me. I am told this is “content streaming”.
src.t.1c1l98m: I drove into a fence and ended up in the river. Then the river was a texture. Explain.

src.t.s0j69t: Not bad. Not Oscar. Not even a Golden Simit.

src.t.1o178oi: My nephew did better in a spreadsheet. Frame by frame.
src.t.1dkvt3d: Sixty frames a second. I counted. Twice. Can it run on my microwave?

src.t.1h4jd40: Databases. A drawer with a lock. Everyone has one. *We* keep our customers on Rıza’s napkin. That ends today.
src.t.t4makp: It’s called *PostGrease*. Like the elephant one, but it slides in. Open source. Legal says that means free. Legal is still my cousin.
src.t.hkhxi0: Rows go in, rows come out, fast, forever, even if I trip over the cable. I tripped over it yesterday. It was not a good day for the napkin.
src.t.19sx588: Tea, anyone? Tip: “fast” and “forever” pull in opposite directions. The whole database is how it pays for the second one without losing the first.
src.t.1f7yi9o: I’ll do the indexes. Someone take the log? And please don’t let me near the cable.
src.t.1z0ciaf: Imagine my tea ledger, sorted by name, split into pages. A page at the top says “A to F is on page 3, G to M on page 4”. You never read the whole book: you read the top page, then the middle one, then the page with your name.
src.t.9enoud: Each page holds hundreds of names, so three levels already hold millions. When a page fills up, cut it in the middle, give each half its own page, and tell the page above where the line is. Cut it carelessly and a name falls in the crack.
src.t.9qutqq: Before I change the big ledger I write one line in my small notebook: “Kaan paid two lira”. The notebook is quick, always the last page. Only later do I bother with the big ledger.
src.t.2j29br: If I drop the tray halfway through, the notebook says exactly what to redo. “Committed” means the notebook line is on the disk, not a promise in my head.
src.t.1hbsv65: When a program writes to a file, the operating system says “yes, yes” and keeps it in memory to write later, like a waiter who nods and writes the order down at the end of the night.
src.t.9mr4c0: *fsync* is you standing there until the paper is in the kitchen. It takes a couple of milliseconds, and it is the difference between “committed” and “committed, probably”. Pull the plug without it and the last seconds are simply gone.
src.t.1e2g8cl: To find every glass with “Kars” on it, I could use the index card and fetch each glass one by one from the shelf. Or I could walk along the shelf and check every glass. For three glasses, the card wins.
src.t.1pk9qgx: For half the glasses, walking the shelf is faster than running back and forth. The planner guesses how many match, adds up the costs of both ways, and picks the cheaper. Always using the index is not always faster.
src.t.7xetds: It is the tea tray at my elbow. The disk is the kitchen, and most customers want the same few glasses, so the tray stays full of those.
src.t.o1w2zn: A bigger tray means fewer walks to the kitchen. But if the tray is bigger than the table, I trip over it: use more memory than the box has and the machine starts swapping, which is slower than the disk you were avoiding.
src.t.1o2a1gk: Two waiters both read “sugar: 100 cubes” on the board. One takes 30 and writes 70. The other takes 20 and writes 80. The board now says 80 and fifty cubes have gone. That is a *lost update*.
src.t.1gsvogy: Isolation levels decide how much of each other’s work they see. With *repeatable read* each waiter works on a snapshot, and when the second one tries to write over a change made since his snapshot, he is stopped and does it again. No cubes lost. A bit slower.
src.t.u4o66p: A replica is a second notebook in another building, copied from the first. *Async*: I tell the customer “done” and copy later. If my building burns down in between, the last few lines are lost.
src.t.1t086r9: *Sync*: I wait until the other building says it has it. A few milliseconds slower for every commit, and a fire loses nothing. Which one you want depends on how much you love the last few seconds of data.
src.t.199lwjc: SQL in, planner, index, log, pages, disk. Eight boxes. Everything in the disk box is the thing the boss is worried about.
src.t.qbjxr8: A query arrives as text: what you want, not how to find it. Finding it is the database’s whole job.
src.t.19l8lw8: Many plans give the same answer at very different costs. The planner estimates each and picks the cheapest: an index for a few rows, a full scan for a big share of the table.
src.t.hgmyj2: Many sessions run at once. Isolation says how much of each other’s half-finished work they may see, and what happens when two touch the same row.
src.t.1iu29vs: A cache of pages in memory. Most queries ask for the same few pages, so a good-sized pool answers most without touching the disk.
src.t.13j0k2t: A tree of sorted pages. A lookup walks from the root down: three or four pages for ten million rows. When a page fills it splits, and the split must not lose a key.
src.t.bvihcp: Every change is written to a log first. A commit is a promise that the log is safe on disk. After a crash the log rebuilds what the pages were missing.
src.t.aih7b3: The tables themselves. Pages are written back lazily; a checkpoint flushes all the dirty ones so recovery has less log to replay.
src.t.rpmr66: Copies that follow the log. They take read traffic, and one of them takes over when the primary dies. Whether the primary waits for them is the safety-versus-speed knob.
src.t.lywlk9: Demo time. Show me PostGrease. And it better not crash.
src.t.12phzb6: PostGrease. The database that remembers everything, if the power stays on. The boss wants it live by Friday.

src.t.1v563rf: The z-buffer: one number per pixel, the nearest depth drawn there so far. A new triangle only wins if it is nearer.
src.t.ho8bw4: A graph is a map made of dots and arrows: the intersections are the dots, the streets are the arrows between them.
src.t.1faqsox: g.add draws one arrow from one intersection to another. A two-way street needs two arrows, a one-way street only one.
src.t.1kqipad: The road file marks one-way streets with this flag: they may be driven from a to b, never back.
src.t.10ahlq2: The length of the street in kilometres. The router turns it into minutes later, when it knows how fast the traffic is.
src.t.1hlrc6s: The guess is A*’s hunch of how long is left to B. Honest hunches keep the answer exact; a hunch that is too big hurries to a worse answer.
src.t.5n1pxs: straightKm is the distance as a crow flies. No road can be shorter than that, which is what makes it a safe base for a guess.
src.t.19it2l7: TOP_SPEED is the fastest any road can be driven. Distance divided by it is the least time any trip could possibly take.
src.t.1uwyevb: A min-heap always hands you the smallest item first. The router keeps its to-do list in one: cheapest-looking intersection next.
src.t.29ktb2: relax asks: is going through this intersection a cheaper way to reach the next one than what I know? If so, remember it.
src.t.5r2loq: Each intersection remembers where it was reached from. pathTo walks that chain backwards from B to A, and that is the route.
src.t.1o8uoul: cost turns a street into minutes: its length over the speed right now. This is where the traffic model plugs in.
src.t.1u4zamh: normalise makes two spellings comparable before they are compared: lower case, and maybe the Turkish letters folded to plain ones.
src.t.1gu6qbq: asciiFold turns ş into s, ı into i, ö into o. People on a phone without a Turkish keyboard type it that way.
src.t.1bo8pwc: MAX_EDITS is how many wrong letters a search may have and still count. Too few and typos fail; too many and Moskova becomes Moda.
src.t.1thwdet: editDistance counts the fewest letters you must add, remove or change to turn one word into the other. Taksm to Taksim is one.
src.t.1pckzbl: With this on, “Kadık” already finds Kadıköy: the words that start with what you typed so far.
src.t.g2lews: When two places are equally close to what you typed, take the one more people go to. Ties are broken by the crowd.
src.t.1y5rsog: prerender is the deepest zoom level drawn in advance. Every level below it is ready before anyone asks; deeper ones wait for a visitor.
src.t.kli0q0: Lazy means draw a tile the first time somebody asks, then keep it. The second visitor gets it instantly.
src.t.13bpgz2: Picture tiles are finished images. Vector tiles are the road lines and the phone draws them: much smaller, a little work for the phone.
src.t.1f9qaog: The route cache keeps the answers to trips people ask again and again. Taksim to Kadıköy is asked a thousand times a minute.
src.t.31q80t: ttl is how many seconds a cached route is kept. Long means more hits but older traffic; short means fresh ETAs and more work.
src.t.6gqy37: The order book is two lists: everyone who wants to buy, best price first, and everyone who wants to sell, best price first.
src.t.1k3q7cf: crosses asks: does the best price on the other side meet this order? A buy at 50.02 crosses a seller at 50.01. A buy at 49.90 does not.
src.t.4y833e: A level is everyone waiting at one price. bestLevel is the queue at the best price on the other side.
src.t.nzi9y8: sortBy puts the queue in the order we will serve it. Whoever is first after sorting is filled first.
src.t.16v0dcq: seq is the order’s arrival number, stamped by the exchange. A smaller seq means you were there first.
src.t.708dya: Pro-rata: split the incoming order between everyone in the queue by how big their orders are. Fair to the big, not to the early.
src.t.aahzb0: rem is what is left of the order to fill. The loop runs until it is zero or nobody on the other side will trade with it.
src.t.tid6s7: takeFrom walks the queue in the order we just chose, trading at each resting order’s own price, until the incoming order is done.
src.t.jcm5o8: Basis points: a hundredth of a percent. 30 of them is 0.30%, charged to whoever takes a price that was waiting.
src.t.1duqmb8: A negative fee is a rebate. Whoever puts a price in the book and waits is paid for it: the exchange needs people who wait.
src.t.bvrgit: bps is the rate in basis points. qty times px is the money that changed hands, in cents; times bps over ten thousand is the fee.
src.t.63chao: 10,000 basis points make one whole. Dividing by it turns a rate in basis points into a fraction.
src.t.19nyxi0: px is the price in whole cents: $50.03 is 5003. No decimals anywhere in the money.
src.t.1k8jdx5: You cannot charge a fraction of a cent. round goes to the nearest cent, floor always goes down. Decide once, on every fill.
src.t.s7zp7a: BAND is how far from the reference price a limit price may be: 0.05 means five percent either way. A zero too many is nine hundred percent.
src.t.1rzvcqk: MAX_QTY is the biggest order we accept. Real funds send twenty thousand shares; a typo sends a hundred and fifty thousand.
src.t.9xy7ev: The reference price is what the market has recently been: the median of the latest orders. The band is measured from it.
src.t.zhyalf: Runs before the order touches the book. Rejecting here costs nothing; letting a silly order trade costs everyone.
src.t.1ey6udr: How big a move is too big: 0.05 means five percent. Too small and the market stops for every piece of news.
src.t.129bhk9: The window is how far back the move is measured: five percent in five minutes is a cliff, five percent in a day is a Tuesday.
src.t.1tzhxpg: How long trading stops. Long enough for people to think and quotes to come back; short enough that the day is not lost.
src.t.1wfo9j6: Shards: the symbols are split between engines, one engine per shard. One symbol can never be split, so the busy one stays on one engine.
src.t.1yip0rn: The journal is the engine’s diary on disk. After a crash it replays the diary and nobody’s order is lost. How often it is written is the question.
src.t.1orfw5p: IDLE_RPM is the speed we want, 850. n_est is the speed the ECU believes in, worked out from the crank sensor. Target minus estimate is the error, and the whole controller is about making it zero.
src.t.1is0bzu: The proportional part: the bigger the error right now, the more the valve moves. Quick, but it needs an error to push, so on its own it never quite gets back to the target.
src.t.1rllo4i: The integral part adds up the error over time, so a small error that lasts still builds up enough push to remove itself. Danger: while the valve is stuck at its end stop it keeps adding up for nothing, and overshoots later. That is called windup.
src.t.pkyu9g: U_BASE is the valve opening that holds idle on a warm engine with nothing switched on. U_AC is the extra opening we already know the A/C compressor will need, so we give it before the revs fall: feed-forward.
src.t.1djeup5: The A/C request, a signal the ECU gets before the compressor clutch closes.
src.t.1sa2m2r: iac_duty is how long the idle air valve is open, in per cent. It has end stops: fully closed and fully open. Asking for more than that changes nothing.
src.t.123ihj2: The time between two runs of this function: the control task period, in seconds.
src.t.1o480n1: The grid lines of the table: the engine speeds down the side, the loads across the top. The table only holds numbers at the crossings.
src.t.1r2rmvy: Finds which square of the grid the point is in: the grid line before it. The next one is index + 1.
src.t.k9m09m: Takes the closest grid crossing and uses its number as is. Cheap, but the answer jumps whenever you cross the halfway line between two crossings.
src.t.ws4bbl: How far between the two grid lines the point is, from 0 to 1. At 0.5 you are in the middle and the answer is the average.
src.t.b73566: Linear interpolation: a slide between two numbers. Do it along the load twice, then once along the speed, and you have a bilinear lookup.
src.t.z35s20: The table’s size. The last row is N_ROWS − 1; one past it is the next thing in memory, which is not a spark angle.
src.t.16rqp10: How long, in milliseconds, a signal has to be bad before the ECU believes it. Crank 40, throttle 200, CAN 40.
src.t.14zpfgd: The debounce counter, one per watched signal. It counts bad time up, and good time down.
src.t.hhjsd6: True if, at this moment, the signal is out of range or does not make sense. A single glitch makes it true once.
src.t.2ert70: Stores the diagnostic trouble code and turns on the reaction: limp-home mode, a lit warning lamp.
src.t.1mnoo5k: Which byte of a 16-bit number goes first on the wire. Big endian (Motorola) sends the high byte first, little endian (Intel) the low one. If the sender and the receiver disagree, 3000 rpm turns into 12 000.
src.t.1uojgp1: How many rpm one bit is worth. The receiver multiplies the raw number by its own value, so the two must be the same number.
src.t.1fwxzh8: Raw bytes cannot be negative. An offset of −40 means raw 0 is −40 °C, so a frozen engine can be reported.
src.t.1o6uaca: How often the frame is sent. A needle that is a second old is no needle.
src.t.175o3zy: End-to-end protection: a counter that goes up in every frame shows lost frames, and a CRC8 over the bytes shows frames damaged on the wire, which the receiver then ignores.
src.t.exwj7k: The period of the control task: injection, spark and idle valve are recomputed this often. A shorter period reacts faster and costs more CPU.
src.t.1l00j5n: The period of the diagnostic task: the sensor checks and fault counters. Faults can be found no faster than this, and the debounce counts in steps of it.
src.t.1rqh5e: Cooperative: a task runs until it is finished, even if a more urgent one is waiting. Preemptive priority: the urgent task cuts in at once, and the interrupted one carries on after.
src.t.j2bjsf: A guard dog in the chip. The control task feeds it every run; if it goes hungry for this long, the dog resets the whole ECU.
src.t.c5sc1w: L1 and L2 are the lengths of the two arm segments: 30 and 25 centimetres. With them and the target, you have a triangle.
src.t.12s4hdc: c2 is the cosine of the elbow angle, from the law of cosines: three sides of a triangle (the two segments and the line to the target) fix its angles.
src.t.wqd5vw: acos turns that cosine back into an angle. A cosine has two angles, plus and minus: elbow up and elbow down. And acos only exists for numbers from −1 to 1.
src.t.3tuair: The number is squeezed into −1 … 1. A target that is too far away then gives a fully stretched arm that points at it, instead of NaN.
src.t.159fctt: atan2 gives the direction of a point as an angle. The shoulder points at the target, minus what the bent elbow takes away.
src.t.1i3swrn: t1 is the shoulder angle and t2 the elbow angle, in radians. Two numbers are all the firmware needs to know where the arm is.
src.t.1nw33ul: kp, the proportional gain: how much current for each radian of error. A stiff spring.
src.t.15z8eot: The integral adds up the error over time, so a small error that stays eventually pushes hard. It is what finally holds the weight of the arm.
src.t.wb1vcy: kd, the derivative gain: a damper. It pushes against the speed, so the arm arrives calmly instead of ringing like a bell.
src.t.1u0vf0p: A low-pass filter smooths a signal. The encoder counts in steps, so its speed jumps between zero and a lot; the filter keeps what is slow and drops the jitter.
src.t.16873ah: The joint speed, from the difference of two encoder readings divided by the time between them. dv is the filtered one.
src.t.1w6th50: The previous encoder reading, kept to compute the speed. It is the measurement, not the error: it does not jump when the setpoint does.
src.t.54ohys: The previous error. The derivative of the error jumps when the setpoint jumps: a derivative kick, a huge push for one tick.
src.t.1h2440q: The anti-windup clamp: the integral may be at most 60% of full current. Without it, the integral keeps filling while the motor is already at its limit.
src.t.1ug989q: dt is the time between two control ticks: a thousandth of a second at 1 kHz. Speeds and sums are all scaled by it.
src.t.oe0maj: The soft limits of each joint, a little inside the hard stops. Past them, the arm is where no arm should be.
src.t.nhwc0j: A fault is anything wrong: the emergency stop is pressed, a joint is past its limit, or a command is not a number.
src.t.lkx75d: The big red mushroom button. Somebody will press it while shouting, and it must work every single time.
src.t.1jm8tli: NaN is “not a number”: the result of a maths mistake, like the arc cosine of 1.2. A motor command that is NaN cannot be trusted.
src.t.2dcurx: Cuts the current to the motors. Alone it lets the arm fall, which is why it comes with the brake.
